blocks.text: The simpler variant. The problem hands you the width `k`, and the window never changes size — it just walks along the array.

The one line people get wrong is `arr[right - k]`. Convince yourself with a concrete case: with `k = 3` and `right = 3`, the entering element is index 3 and the leaving one is index 0. The window was {0,1,2} and becomes {1,2,3}. `right - k = 0`. Correct.
The general rule: when `right` is the newest index, the window covers `right - k + 1` through `right`, so the element that just fell out is at `right - k`.
Why the loop starts at k

The first window — indices 0 through k−1 — is built by the initial loop. The sliding loop handles everything after, so it starts at `k`, the first index not already included. Starting at 0 would double-count.
A running sum is only the simplest case. The same skeleton works for anything you can update incrementally:

items: **Count of something** — increment when it enters, decrement when it leaves.
**Character frequencies** — a map updated by two keys per step.

blocks.text: The thing that must stay constant-time is the update. If maintaining your window state costs O(k) per step, the whole thing degrades back to O(N x k).
**Time: O(N)** — one pass to build, one pass to slide, constant work per step.
**Space: O(1)** for a sum, or O(k) if you track the window's contents in a map.
